title: Auditors slam ‘stalled’ EU clean energy plans, urge investments boost – Batteries International
content: EU plans to supercharge the clean energy transition and wean the bloc off Russian gas and oil have stalled — and not enough investments are being made in vital projects, a shock new report has warned. It is also unclear how much Russian oil has dodged sanctions and made its way into the European market, according to a European Court of Auditors (ECA) report published on September 9. The ECA’s intervention came just seven months after auditors slammed EU chiefs over supplies of metals and minerals critical to battery manufacturing and other sectors, saying moves to diversify supply chains had yet to show tangible results. Now, the ECA has targeted the REPowerEU plan — launched in 2022 to secure energy independence from Russian oil and gas imports in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine. The plan has effectively stalled because it does not provide for effective governance to monitor the implementation and progress of projects, the auditors said. Battery storage Under REPowerEU, battery storage is designated as a core enabler of Europe’s clean‑energy transition, with around 55GW installed and 30GW more in the pipeline as of April 2026. According to the auditors the plan “is struggling to deliver”, just as Europe’s energy security is facing renewed threats from the turmoil in the Middle East. And while EU sanctions have led to a drastic fall in imports of oil from Russia, the auditors said it is unclear how much has been imported via third countries or through ‘shadow fleet’ tankers. Gas imports have also fallen, but some EU countries imported more Russian gas in 2024 than before the outbreak of the war in Ukraine, the auditors said. The drop in Russian energy imports can also be attributed to other factors, such as a series of mild winters and lower consumption due to high energy prices. This means that the REPowerEU plan’s direct impact might be more modest than it first appears. Ambitious goals The plan included accelerated permitting rules for all energy storage projects, including standalone and co-located renewable energy facilities. But without a major boost, the auditors have warned REPowerEU will be unable to reach its ambitious goals. The plan has had little resonance so far across national policies, as the 27 EU member states have committed not even a fifth of the €300 billion ($348 billion) in additional investments needed to meet its objectives, the auditors said. The European Commission had estimated that some €300 billion in additional investments would be required by 2030 — and made this amount available from the Covid pandemic ‘recovery cash pot’, the recovery and resilience facility (RRF). Member states could add dedicated REPowerEU operations to their recovery plans for delivering the plan’s objectives, but auditors said the governance framework lacks effective tools to steer the implementation of the plan and reliably track results. ‘Huge gap’ Individual EU nations’ national energy and climate plans were meant to steer REPowerEU but in reality most did not include any specific actions or targets to bolster the plan’s objectives. “In addition, EU countries committed only €54.3 billion out of the €300 billion made available under the RRF for REPowerEU. For the auditors, such a huge gap indicates either that investment needs were wrongly estimated and largely overblown, or that there is an inability to translate objectives into concrete action.” While the plan has helped to speed up some key projects in member states, it has done little to accelerate the clean energy transition by increasing renewable production capacity. Based on the targets included in the dedicated RRF chapters, the auditors found that the additional renewables production capacity created is negligible and very far from the 103GW objective. The same observation applies to grid interconnectivity. The EU auditors identified only three REPowerEU measures across two member states for this target, and one was eventually dropped. ECA member Mihails Kozlovs, who spearheaded the report, said: “Four years after its launch, REPowerEU has stalled, even though several hundred billion euros have been made available. Highly critical “We must learn the right lessons now, as the new geopolitical tensions and their impact on energy markets underscore the need to accelerate diversification and prevent future over-reliance on a single supplier.” The auditors’ findings are the latest in a string of recent reports that have been highly critical of the EU. Last March, plans for the rollout of much needed energy storage capacity across Europe were criticised as uneven, fragmented and hindering investment in a study by the EU’s Joint Research Centre. Last month, the block was accused of sidelining sustainability principles in the race to secure materials vital to the battery industry. A study published on August 13, by Germany’s Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research, said security of supply was now taking precedence over sufficiency in raw materials policy. Also in August, analysis from Deloitte claimed Europe’s auto industry could see up to €10.5 billion ($12 billion) in profits diverted to Asia by the end of the decade because of a chronic dependency on sourcing EV battery cells from the the region. Europe’s battery industry is now at a crossroads — and buying cheap battery cells from Asia is not a long-term solution for sovereign European battery production, the report warned. title: ABTC gets green light for Nevada lithium project – Batteries International
content: The American Battery Technology Company said on September 8 the US Bureau of Land Management had given the go-ahead for its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project mine and refinery in Nevadaa. This follows after completing its review of the project — one of the US’s largest known lithium resources. Acceptance of the mine and refinery plan of operations is the culmination of over four years of work, including demonstrating the performance of ABTC’s own technologies for manufacturing high-purity lithium hydroxide. ABTC said Tonopah encompasses one of the largest known measured, indicated and inferred lithium claystone resource deposits in the US. The project is one of a number selected as a federal priority project for streamlined permitting, to aid the Trump administration’s moves to stop the US being exploited by overseas battery supply chain dominance. Tonopah Flats is designed to bolster domestic production of critical minerals needed for grid-scale BESS systems, EVs and datacenters. ABTC chief executive Ryan Melsert said BLM’s certification of the mine and refinery plan of operations was a major accomplishment by his team and a critical milestone in the construction and commercialisation of the project pre-feasibility study of Tonopah published in October 2025 indicated that the project had a highly competitive cost of production of $4,307 per tonne of lithium hydroxide monohydrate. Earlier this year, the US Department of Energy reinstated a grant to support building the project. title: Nano One launches Canada DevCo to spearhead LFP supply chain – Batteries International
content: Nano One said on September 11 it is moving ahead with its first development company, Canada DevCo, as part of plans to deploy LFP cathode production facilities in Canada. The company has launched a site evaluation study to assess possible locations for a proposed 25ktpa cathode production plant, with a potential expansion to up to 100ktpa of production capacity. Nano One said the project aims to serve ESS, EV and defence markets in Canada and internationally. The study will identify preferred site options and assess factors such as access to utilities and key infrastructure, as well as relevant permitting roadmaps. COO Denis Geoffroy said the project would expand the company’s reach beyond its initial Candiac facility in Quebec. “There is increasing market pull from customers for the industry to deliver LFP cathode active materials from a regionally focused and resilient supply chain,” the firm said.  “Discussions with potential strategic partners and customers for Canada DevCo are progressing.” Batteries International reported in November 2025 that Nano One had been awarded C$5 million ($3.6 million) from Natural Resources Canada to scale production of the firm’s proprietary One-Pot process for LFP cathode active materials process and accelerate commercialisation. Canada’s energy and natural resources minister Tim Hodgson said the funding would support Nano One’s work at its Candiac, Québec and Burnaby facilities through to March 31, 2027. In a related move, Ontario province launched a C$500 million ($364 million) critical minerals processing fund to support investment in projects including EV and battery manufacturing. title: India’s NTPC invites partners for sodium ion BESS trials – Batteries International
content: Indian state-owned power utility NTPC is calling for expressions of interest in a pilot project to evaluate grid-connected sodium ion energy storage systems. The BESS systems would be deployed at some of NTPC’s existing thermal power plants and office buildings. NTPC issued the call for expressions of interested on September 9, saying it wanted to hear from companies and tech providers capable of designing, supplying, installing and commissioning the systems. Two capacity options for the pilot project have been proposed. Under the first option, the BESS would need a usable energy capacity of 100kWh at the point of interconnection. Under the second option, applicants can propose their own capacities based on their standard configuration and scale of the demonstration. Safety and fire protection systems should form part of applications in line with statutory requirements. Applicants would also need to indicate the technology readiness level of their proposal, although those below technology readiness level (TRL) 4 will not be considered. For TRL 4 or TRL 5, applicants must contribute a minimum of 50% of the total project cost. For TRL 6 and above, there would be no mandatory minimum contribution. However, the amount would be agreed with NTPC on application. Preference may be given to those who offer a higher financial contribution, the power company said. NTPC will provide land and site support for the pilot project and will also provide a feeder for charging and discharging the BESS and auxiliary power if required. Applicants will retain the intellectual property related to the technology although IP generated through the pilot demonstration will be jointly owned with NTPC, with special provisions for commercialisation in the case of TRL4-5 technologies. The last date for submissions to NTPC is October 15, 2026. The post India’s NTPC invites partners for sodium ion BESS trials appeared first on Batteries International .

title: The hidden chain reaction behind the 2026 Nepal-China flooding disaster
content:
On August 26, 2026, a series of avalanches, flash floods, and debris flows in Nepal and Tibet left an estimated 1,400 people dead, with another 5,850 still missing. Dubbed the 2026 Nepal-China floods, the disaster destroyed the China-Nepal Gyirong checkpoint and devastated dozens of settlements along a 45-mile (72 km) stretch of the Trishuli River.
The event also severely damaged around a dozen hydropower plants, constituting around 10% of Nepal’s total power production.
According to reports
, it is not yet clear if the damage can be repaired.

title: 9 operational US aircraft that can fly faster than sound
content: Supersonic flight is often associated with experimental aircraft, futuristic fighters, and Cold War-era icons. Yet the US still operates a surprisingly broad collection of aircraft that can fly faster than the speed of sound. Most are military aircraft, and there is an important distinction here. An aircraft’s supersonic capability does not mean it routinely cruises at supersonic speeds. In fact, for most modern fighters, sustained supersonic flight is something used selectively because it consumes fuel rapidly and can impose significant thermal and aerodynamic loads. For this list, we are counting aircraft that are currently in US military service and have an officially stated supersonic capability. That includes fighters, an electronic-warfare aircraft, a bomber, and even training and adversary aircraft. It does not include retired aircraft or experimental X-planes. Here are nine of them. 1. F-15 Eagle The F-15 remains one of the US’s fastest operational fighters more than five decades after its first flight. The current US fleet includes the F-15E Strike Eagle , while the newer F-15EX Eagle II is entering service. The F-15E has a stated maximum speed of around Mach 2.5, or roughly 1,875 mph. Its two afterburning engines provide the thrust needed for that performance, although the aircraft rarely flies near its maximum speed in combat. The Eagle’s longevity is also part of the story. Rather than replacing the entire family, the US has continued evolving the design into newer variants with modern sensors, weapons, and avionics. 2. F-16 Fighting Falcon The F-16 is considerably smaller than the F-15, but it is still capable of reaching approximately Mach 2 at altitude. The single-engine fighter entered US service in the late 1970s and remains one of the most numerous tactical aircraft in the US inventory. The Air Force describes it as a compact multirole fighter capable of both air-to-air and air-to-surface missions. That combination of speed, maneuverability, and relatively compact size has made the F-16 one of the most widely operated fighter designs in the world. 3. F-22 Raptor The F-22 Raptor combines supersonic performance with something even more unusual: the ability to cruise supersonically without continuously using afterburners. The Air Force describes the F-22 as a Mach 2-class aircraft with supercruise capability. It can cruise above Mach 1.5 without afterburner, potentially covering ground much faster than a conventional fighter operating below the sound barrier. The Raptor was designed primarily as an air-superiority fighter, with stealth, sensor fusion, and maneuverability playing as important a role as raw speed. 4. F-35 Lightning II The F-35 is not the fastest aircraft on this list, but all three US variants are supersonic: the F-35A, F-35B, and F-35C. Their published maximum speed is approximately Mach 1.6. The F-35B is particularly unusual because it combines supersonic flight with short takeoff and vertical landing capability, allowing the Marine Corps to operate it from amphibious ships and austere bases. The F-35’s design prioritizes stealth, sensors, and networking over extreme speed, so Mach 1.6 is better viewed as a capability than its normal operating regime. 5. F/A-18E/F Super Hornet The US Navy’s F/A-18E/F Super Hornet is another carrier-based supersonic fighter. NAVAIR lists its maximum airspeed as Mach 1.8+. The twin-engine aircraft serves as a multirole fighter and attack platform aboard US aircraft carriers. Unlike some older carrier aircraft, the Super Hornet was designed from the beginning around the demands of modern carrier operations, combining supersonic performance with weapons carriage, range, and multirole flexibility. 6. EA-18G Growler The EA-18G Growler looks remarkably similar to the Super Hornet because it is derived from the F/A-18F. Its job, however, is very different. The Growler is the US Navy’s dedicated airborne electronic-warfare aircraft, designed to disrupt and attack hostile radar and communications systems while supporting other aircraft. Despite carrying specialized electronic-warfare equipment, it retains the Super Hornet’s basic high-performance characteristics. US Navy material lists a maximum speed of approximately Mach 1.8. 7. B-1B Lancer Not all operational US supersonic aircraft are fighters. The B-1B Lancer is a long-range strategic bomber capable of reaching approximately Mach 1.2, according to the Air Force. Its variable-sweep wings let it change configuration for different parts of the flight envelope. That makes the B-1B a rather unusual aircraft on this list. It is vastly larger than the fighters above, yet can still cross the sound barrier. 8. T-38 Talon Supersonic capability is not limited to combat aircraft. The US Air Force’s T-38 Talon is a two-seat supersonic trainer used to prepare pilots for high-performance aircraft. The design first flew in the 1950s, making it one of the oldest aircraft designs still serving in the US military. Yet its ability to provide high-speed jet training has kept it relevant for generations of pilots. Its continued presence is a useful reminder that an aircraft does not have to be a frontline fighter to be operationally important—or supersonic. 9. F-5 Tiger II The F-5N/F Tiger II occupies another unusual niche. Although the original F-5 is decades old, the US Navy and Marine Corps continue operating upgraded examples primarily as adversary aircraft, giving US pilots a representative target to train against. The lightweight fighter is capable of supersonic flight, with the F-5 family capable of reaching roughly Mach 1.6. In other words, the US still operates a supersonic aircraft whose primary job is to pretend to be the enemy. What about the X-planes and commercial? This list leaves out some of the most interesting US supersonic aircraft because they are experimental rather than operational. The clearest current example is NASA’s X-59, which broke the sound barrier for the first time in June 2026 and subsequently continued its flight-test campaign. The US also has a long history of X-planes exploring everything from supersonic flight to hypersonics. So while today’s operational fleet is dominated by military aircraft, America’s supersonic story is far from being confined to fighters and bombers. In fact, The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is working to lift the 53-year-old ban on overland commercial supersonic flights in the U.S. by mid-2027. The next major chapter may instead be about making supersonic flight quieter, more efficient, and potentially useful for civilian travel.

title: 911 for humanoids: Japan debuts first-ever ‘robot ambulance’ to provide on-site repairs
content: Japanese tech giant GMO Internet Group (GMO Air) has just unveiled what has been dubbed Japan’s first “robot ambulance.” Effectively a kind of roadside assistance for humanoid robots, the new vehicle will soon be put to work on the streets of Tokyo. The specially equipped van is designed to carry engineers, repair equipment, replacement parts, and a spare humanoid robot to sites when and where needed. “The humanoid ‘ambulance’ carries the replacement humanoid to the site and replaces it with the damaged humanoid,” explained Shota Takizawa, an engineer at GMO Air . The idea would be that if the “ambulance” can’t effect a repair on site, the robot can either be ferried back to a “repair base” with the replacement acting like a “courtesy car” robot for the customer. Importantly, the van isn’t autonomous , and it isn’t a robot repairing another robot by itself, making it an interesting blend of old and new. To imagine it in action, consider a hotel with two humanoid cleaning “staff” or a warehouse with humanoid “workers.” If one of these robots breaks down at the start of the working day, then the customer would lose several days of service if the robot is sent back to GMO Air for repairs. Tokyo to get nation’s first “robot ambulance” The new service will effectively compress the repair timeline by bringing engineers and parts to the customer on site. These engineers will then diagnose the problem on site, repair it if possible, or leave another robot as they take the old one away to fix. That’s actually quite a sensible service model if humanoids become common. Once businesses depend upon them to perform work, uptime, field maintenance, spare-parts logistics and replacement machines become important. It’s exactly the kind of ecosystem that developed around cars, industrial machinery, aircraft and IT hardware. With this new vehicle, GMO is imagining a future where humanoid robots are doing commercially important jobs in factories, shops, offices, warehouses, etc. The problem is that if a £50k–£100k-ish robot breaks down, you don’t necessarily want to ship it back to a service center and leave the customer’s operation without it for days. Roadside assistance for humanoid robots According to GMO Air, the concept was borne out of its experience with disruptions when damaged robots needed to be sent away for repair. “Learning from that experience, we came up with the idea of providing replacement humanoids,” Tomohiro Uchida, CEO of GMO Air, said. “When humanoids become more popular, this kind of service will be needed,” Takizawa added. At present, there is just a single “ambulance” available at GMO Air’s Tokyo headquarters. But they add that they plan to add many more vehicles in the future if customer demand justifies it. Presently, the singular vehicle is a demonstration/pilot of a field-support business GMO thinks may be necessary as humanoid deployment increases. Its unveiling also comes amidst growing competition between nations for humanoid robot development, especially in the US and China. Japan’s government, for its part, has recently set a target of 10 million robots to be in service by 2040 across multiple industries from healthcare to manufacturing. If anything remotely approaching that scale happens, mundane stuff like “ Who comes out when my robot’s left knee actuator craps itself?” could become a surprisingly large industry.

title: 7 humanoid robot makers taking over real-world factories
content: Humanoid robots are steadily moving out of research laboratories and into factories, warehouses, customer-service centers, and other human-built environments. Equipped with artificial intelligence, these machines are learning to understand instructions, recognize objects, navigate complex spaces, and perform physical tasks. American companies remain influential in developing advanced AI models, robotic hardware, and general-purpose machines. However, Chinese manufacturers have established a substantial lead in production and accounted for more than four out of every five humanoid robot installations worldwide in 2025. 1. Figure AI Wikimedia Commons California-based Figure AI is developing general-purpose humanoids that can work inside factories before eventually expanding into homes. Its latest Figure 03 robot is powered by Helix, an embodied AI system that converts visual information and natural-language instructions into physical actions. Figure has already demonstrated its technology on an active BMW production line rather than limiting it to carefully arranged demonstrations. Figure 02 loaded more than 90,000 components, accumulated over 1,250 operating hours, and contributed to the production of more than 30,000 vehicles. 2. AgiBot Wikimedia Commons Founded in Shanghai in 2023, AgiBot has quickly emerged as one of China’s largest producers of embodied AI robots. Its portfolio includes full-size humanoids, industrial machines, service robots, quadrupeds, and open platforms that researchers can use to develop new applications. AgiBot led the global market with 30.4 percent of installations in 2025, according to figures covered by the South China Morning Post . Its success has been driven by mass production, an open-source strategy, and robots designed for manufacturing, logistics, entertainment, research, and customer-facing roles. 3. Unitree Robotics Wikimedia Commons Unitree Robotics initially became known for its agile quadruped robots before entering the humanoid market with machines such as the H1 and G1. The company’s biggest strengths include balance control, powerful compact actuators, dynamic movement, and relatively affordable hardware. Its G1 humanoid starts at approximately $13,500, making advanced robotic hardware more accessible to universities, developers, and AI laboratories. Unitree captured 26.4 percent of worldwide humanoid installations in 2025 and has attracted attention with robots that can run, dance, maintain balance, and perform complex movements. 4. Tesla Tesla is developing Optimus as a general-purpose humanoid capable of handling unsafe, repetitive, and physically demanding activities. The robot uses technologies related to the company’s autonomous vehicles, including computer vision, neural networks, batteries, electric motors, and real-world navigation systems. Tesla also possesses something most robotics start-ups lack: experience manufacturing complicated machines at enormous scale. However, Optimus has yet to achieve significant commercial deployment, and Elon Musk has acknowledged that its initial production ramp will be extremely slow. 5. UBTech Robotics Wikimedia Commons Shenzhen-based UBTech Robotics is targeting practical industrial work with its Walker series of full-size humanoid robots. These machines are being developed for automotive manufacturing, material handling, quality inspection, component sorting, logistics, and repetitive assembly operations. The Walker S2 can replace its own battery, helping it resume work without relying on a person to connect it to a charger. UBTech shipped 1,079 full-size humanoids in 2025, although a Reuters investigation found that humanoids generally remain too slow and error-prone for most industrial work. 6. Apptronik Texas-based Apptronik traces its origins to robotic projects connected to NASA’s Valkyrie humanoid program. Its Apollo robot is designed to perform activities including moving materials, delivering components, inspecting products, tending machines, assembling kits, and completing warehouse orders. Apptronik has secured commercial agreements with Mercedes-Benz and logistics company GXO while partnering with Google DeepMind to integrate Gemini-based intelligence. The company has also raised more than $935 million, giving it substantial resources to improve Apollo and establish large-scale manufacturing operations. 7. Boston Dynamics Boston Dynamics has spent decades developing robots capable of performing movements that once appeared impossible for machines. Its fully electric Atlas humanoid combines powerful actuators, flexible joints, advanced perception, autonomous mobility, and hands designed to manipulate objects inside industrial environments. The Hyundai-owned company is now transforming Atlas from an experimental platform into a commercially useful manufacturing robot. It is also working with Google DeepMind on AI capabilities, while Hyundai plans to introduce production versions of Atlas at its factories. Humanoid robots still have work to do Despite their rapid progress, today’s humanoids cannot match people at handling unpredictable situations or completing varied tasks without assistance. Specialized industrial robots can also perform many structured factory operations faster, more reliably, and at a lower cost. Still, all companies are steadily narrowing that gap. Their biggest test will not be making humanoids dance or perform impressive demonstrations, but proving that these machines can deliver reliable economic value in the real world.

title: Brazil’s 1.1-billion-ton rare earth project hits peak 95% terbium recovery in lab tests
content: Rare earths are increasingly becoming a supply-chain issue rather than simply a mining story, particularly for elements such as terbium and dysprosium that are used to improve the performance of permanent magnets at high temperatures. Brazilian company IMC Rare Earths says laboratory testing at its Itarantim project has produced terbium recoveries of up to 95.2%, alongside the successful production of a mixed rare earth carbonate. The results could strengthen the case for developing the project as another source of magnet materials outside China, although the work remains at the laboratory testing stage. Itarantim is an ionic adsorption clay deposit spanning Bahia and Minas Gerais and is estimated to contain about 1.1 billion tonnes of inferred mineral resources. The company says the resource contains neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium . Combining high terbium recovery with rare earth carbonate production The latest results came from metallurgical testwork conducted with the Instituto Federal do Rio Grande do Norte and its EMBRAPII-affiliated CT Mineral laboratory. In the best-performing composite, known as COMP C2, terbium recovery averaged 81.1% and reached a maximum of 95.2%. Recovery, rather than simply the concentration of an element in the ground, is an important indicator of whether a deposit could eventually be processed economically. For ionic adsorption clay deposits, rare earth elements are loosely attached to clay minerals and can be released through leaching. IMC says material from a 105.8 million tonne inferred domain at Itarantim contains an average of 8 parts per million terbium. The company also reported strong leach recoveries for other magnet rare earth elements, including dysprosium . “Terbium and dysprosium are among the scarcest and most highly sought-after elements,” the company said in a statement, pointing to their use in permanent magnets for EVs, wind turbines, robotics , electronics and defense systems. Brazil aims for a bigger role in rare earth supply The strategic importance of the project comes from the concentration of rare earth processing and refining capacity in China . While rare earth elements are found in multiple countries, building alternative supply chains requires deposits with suitable geology, extraction characteristics and processing economics. That has turned projects in countries such as Brazil, Australia, the US and Canada into potential components of a more diversified supply chain. Brazil is already one of the world’s major mineral producers , while its rare earth sector has attracted growing interest as governments and companies look for alternatives to Chinese supply. “We are very encouraged by these results, which mark an important step forward in our project. There has been an awakening around the world that we need greater supplies of rare earths from diverse areas,” said Frank Scolaro, CEO and chair of IMC Rare Earths. While the scale of the resource is notable, the project still needs additional technical work before its commercial potential can be established. IMC has now brought in ANSTO Minerals for additional quantitative metallurgical testing, and the next phase is expected to provide more detailed data on recovery rates and the properties of the mixed rare earth carbonate produced from Itarantim material.

title: Bill Gates-backed nuclear fusion firm gets Hyundai Motor backing in $1 billion raise
content: Bill Gates-backed US nuclear fusion firm Commonwealth Fusion Systems has secured an investment from South Korea’s Hyundai Motor Group to help build its commercial power stations. The funding was completed as part of a recent $1 billion capital raise, which will allow both organisations to explore engineering partnerships for commercial fusion power stations known as ARC. “Fusion energy has the potential to play an important role in addressing growing global energy demand while supporting a more sustainable future,” said Hokeun Chung, Executive Vice President of Hyundai Motor Group. The core technology behind the project relies on a machine known as a tokamak. This nuclear fusion device is a donut-shaped chamber, which uses powerful magnetic fields to confine superheated plasma. To make nuclear fusion viable, CFS relies on high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets. These advanced superconducting magnets create significantly stronger magnetic fields while remaining relatively compact. This magnetic strength enables the reactor to keep the high-energy plasma stable inside a much smaller vessel. This magnet design was first developed for SPARC, a net-energy demonstration tokamak currently undergoing assembly at the company’s facility in Devens, Massachusetts. The ARC commercial plant will directly scale up this high-temperature superconducting architecture. Physical validity of hardware approach The physical validity of this hardware approach received formal scientific confirmation in June 2026. Following a peer-reviewed research study, CFS verified the core plasma physics assumptions governing the ARC design. According to the validated models, the ARC plant will produce approximately 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of fusion power to generate 400 megawatts (MW) of net electricity for the grid. “CFS is focused on completing the assembly of its SPARC fusion demonstration machine in Devens, Massachusetts, and also continues to move forward with development of the world’s first grid-scale ARC fusion power plant at the company’s Fall Line Fusion Power Station in Chesterfield County, Virginia,” noted the US fusion firm. Preparing for operational power delivery To prepare for operational power delivery, CFS submitted an interconnection application to PJM Interconnection, the operator running the largest wholesale electricity market in the United States. It marks the first time a fusion developer has filed formal paperwork to link directly into the regional high-voltage grid. Commercial framework agreements for the Virginia facility are already in place ahead of its scheduled startup in the early 2030s. Regional utility Dominion Energy is collaborating on site development, while corporate investors Google and Italian energy supplier Eni have signed long-term power purchase agreements to buy more than half of the plant’s total electrical generation . “As we prepare to put fusion energy on the grid in the early 2030s, we see partnerships with leading industrial and energy companies like Hyundai as an important component to helping us scale our ARC power plant business,” added Bob Mumgaard, CEO and Co-founder of CFS. “CFS has demonstrated strong technical progress toward commercial fusion energy, and we look forward to exploring opportunities to contribute our industrial, engineering and infrastructure expertise as the industry advances,” concluded Chung.

title: Fusion research to get major boost with superconducting tape manufacturing
content: A Munich-based company has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Germany’s State of Lower Saxony. Proxima Fusion’s deal with the state aims at laying foundations for large-scale industrial production of high-temperature superconducting (HTS) tape in Lower Saxony. The new production site is intended to create industrial value and highly skilled jobs, while establishing an essential industrial foundation for new European supply chains. Around €140 million in investment is planned for the first two project phases, running until the end of 2029.Fusion-energy goals“We are making Lower Saxony a pioneer in European HTS manufacturing,” said Olaf Lies, Minister-President of Lower Saxony. “This will not only support Germany’s ambitious fusion-energy goals, but also bring advanced manufacturing, new economic value, highly skilled jobs and technological expertise to our state, with the potential to generate positive innovation effects across many other industries. Lower Saxony will become, quite literally, a magnet for a new critical technology.”HTS tape is a specialized metallic tape that becomes superconducting at relatively high temperatures. In its superconducting state, it can carry electrical currents with virtually no resistive losses, making it possible to build electromagnets that are both exceptionally powerful and compact. The magnets built from the tape are essential to stellarators: they generate the magnetic fields that confine and control the extremely hot plasma inside a fusion machine. This makes HTS tape a key enabling technology for fusion. By enabling more compact and powerful fusion machines, it supports not only the technical realisation of fusion energy, but also the development of cost-effective power plants, according to a press release.The planned production site, which will be the first-of-its-kind in Germany and Europe, will create an essential industrial foundation in Lower Saxony for Proxima’s Alpha fusion demonstrator, its planned Stellaris power plant and, ultimately, the production of stellarators at scale. Beyond supporting the stellarator supply chain, the HTS manufacturing capacity would also serve other applications including high-performance electricity grids, medical imaging and treatment, advanced propulsion systems and other high-field magnet technologies, as per the release.HTS tape is one of critical technologies needed to scale fusionCurrently, HTS tape is manufactured at industrial scale primarily in Asia. Establishing domestic production capacity is strategically important if the stellarator supply chain is to be located almost entirely within Europe. Under current plans, Proxima will require approximately 20,000 kilometres of HTS tape for Alpha and a further 40,000 kilometres for Stellaris. Long-term purchase volumes will be critical to scaling production, retaining manufacturing expertise and reducing the cost per metre.Proxima aims to finance the total investment equally through private capital and public funding, with the State of Lower Saxony providing €21 million, representing just under 30% of the proposed public funding contribution.“HTS tape is one of the critical technologies needed to scale fusion rapidly at an industrial level,” said Dr Francesco Sciortino, co-founder and CEO of Proxima Fusion. “Alpha and Stellaris will create the demand required to build this manufacturing expertise locally. Lower Saxony has the industrial base, energy expertise and political determination to turn a supply-chain dependency into an enduring strategic strength for Germany and Europe.”This plant enables Germany to retain manufacturing expertise and economic value, make its European supply chains more resilient and translate its world-leading stellarator research into an internationally significant industry. By bringing together materials expertise, production processes, quality assurance, skilled workers and suppliers, it would create a critical upstream manufacturing capability with applications across a wide range of sectors while reducing dependence on overseas suppliers, as per the release.“Lower Saxony offers excellent conditions for the industries of the future,” said Falko Mohrs, Minister of Science and Culture, Lower Saxony. “Our research institutions have particular strengths in key fusion technologies, especially laser physics and photonics. The planned facility demonstrates the importance of collaboration between science and industry in developing new areas of strength for Lower Saxony.”

title: US firm boosts counter-drone production with 191,000-square-foot facility
content: In Austin, Texas, Alien Control Systems (ACS) is opening a new 191,000-square-foot manufacturing plant to increase production of its Bullfrog counter-drone system in response to demand from the U.S. and its allies.In a press release, ACS said the new facility will enable the company to quickly scale up production of Bullfrog, the autonomous weapon station it designed to counter low-cost weaponized drones. The expansion will also involve hiring in engineering, manufacturing, quality, testing, and supply chain.“The United States and allied nations have sent us a clear message: they need Bullfrog to safeguard U.S. and allied forces and critical infrastructure from this omnipresent threat, now,” said ACS co-founder and CEO Mike Wior.“We’re building the production capacity, so Bullfrog is at the ready when and where it is needed most, and we’re proud to do our part to support the reindustrialization of American manufacturing in the process,” he added.The Bullfrog system combines computer vision, autonomous control, and precision robotics with existing weapons; ACS said the U.S. Army and Navy have already deployed it, and it has contracts with Joint Interagency Task Force 401 and several allied militaries.The system was also recently selected by the U.S. Marine Corps for its Ground Based Air Defense (GBAD) program, according to ACS.Bullfrog: AI and computer vision to track aerial targetsThe Marine Corps selected Bullfrog for the Light Marine Air Defense Integrated System (LMADIS), an expeditionary, vehicle-based counter-unmanned aircraft system under the broader GBAD program, Tectonic Defense reported.Bullfrog uses artificial intelligence and computer vision to identify and track aerial targets and can be operated alongside a standard M240 machine gun. ACS had obtained more than $120 million in contracts for Bullfrog with the U.S. Special Operations Command, the Navy, the Army and the militaries of various allies, including the United Arab Emirates and South Korea.Bullfrog can be installed on platforms including pickup trucks, unmanned surface vessels and fixed sites, according to Tectonic. While the system was developed with small Group 1 drones in mind, Wior told the publication that Bullfrog had also demonstrated success against larger Group 3 drones.The initial Marine Corps other transaction agreement for Bullfrog was valued at approximately $6.2 million, Tectonic continued. The system can fire up to 850 rounds per minute as part of its integration with LMADIS.“Advanced defense production is a national security imperative,” said ACS Chief Operating Officer Laura Komkov in a press release. “By expanding our manufacturing capabilities and highly skilled workforce, we are further strengthening our ability to produce and deliver mission-critical hardware to the field as quickly as possible.”Counter-drone attack neededThe manufacturing expansion comes as ACS broadens Bullfrog’s use across U.S. military services. In addition to its Marine Corps selection, the system is deployed with U.S. forces, and the company holds contracts with the Army, Marine Corps, Special Operations Command, and Joint Interagency Task Force 401.ACS, headquartered in Austin, also operates offices in Alexandria, Virginia, and an innovation lab in Huntsville, Alabama. The company said the new Texas facility is part of its continued investment in domestic manufacturing capacity and the workforce needed to produce its defense systems at scale.

title: US Army gets next-gen artillery guidance kit built for GPS jamming
content: Northrop Grumman will produce a new version of its Precision Guidance Kit (PGK) designed to keep 155 mm artillery accurate when GPS signals are degraded or jammed. The PGK E5 adds anti-jamming technology to the existing guidance kit while retaining the same form factor and compatibility with fielded artillery systems. The upgrade is intended to let US Army and allied forces continue using GPS-guided artillery in environments where electronic warfare can disrupt satellite navigation. Recent testing in GPS-degraded conditions showed the PGK E5 exceeding both threshold and objective accuracy requirements, the company added.Production is already underway at the company’s facility in Plymouth, Minnesota, with first deliveries expected in early 2028.Getting a precision-guidance upgradeThe PGK E5 is designed to convert existing 155 mm high-explosive artillery projectiles into precision-guided weapons without requiring major changes to the ammunition or the artillery systems firing them. The kit fits onto the front of compatible projectiles and provides GPS-based guidance during flight, allowing artillery crews to achieve greater accuracy than conventional unguided rounds. The new E5 variant adds anti-jamming capabilities intended to maintain that precision when adversaries interfere with GPS signals.Importantly, Northrop Grumman says the upgrade does not change the kit’s fit, form or user experience. It remains compatible with existing 155 mm projectiles and fielded howitzers, meaning troops should not require extensive retraining or modifications to their artillery systems.“Today’s threat environment demands speed and innovation and we’re working closely with the US Army to ensure the PGK E5 keeps maneuver forces ready to win in GPS degraded environments. With decades of proven performance and growing production, PGK continues to deliver reliable, mission-ready technology that warfighters can count on,” said Dave Fine, vice president of armament systems at Northrop Grumman.Designed for contested GPS environmentsThe PGK E5 builds on the M1156 Precision Guidance Kit, which has already been deployed as a way of improving the accuracy of conventional 155 mm artillery ammunition.Northrop Grumman says testing of the new variant in GPS-degraded environments demonstrated accuracy beyond both the Army’s threshold and objective requirements. Greater precision can reduce the number of rounds required to engage a target while potentially limiting unintended damage and reducing the time artillery crews remain exposed to enemy counter-fire.The anti-jamming capability is therefore aimed at preserving the value of existing precision artillery as battlefield electronic warfare becomes more sophisticated. By maintaining reliable guidance even when GPS signals are disrupted, the system could allow forces to continue using precision rounds without relying on major changes to their existing artillery platforms or ammunition.Furthermore, because the system can be integrated with ammunition and artillery already in service, the Army and allied forces can field the upgrade without waiting for an entirely new artillery weapon or major changes to their existing infrastructure.

title: China turns Type 19 into potential mobile laser defense system
content: China may be developing a new version of its Type 19 amphibious 8×8 combat vehicle designed to protect frontline troops from the growing threat posed by drones. Unverified images that appeared on Chinese social media in late August show a Type 19 variant fitted with a turret-mounted laser weapon, additional sensors and its standard autocannon. The vehicle could be particularly relevant to a potential Taiwan conflict, where PLA amphibious forces would face extensive use of drones for surveillance, targeting and direct attacks. If the modified vehicle retains the Type 19’s amphibious capability, it could provide counter-drone protection while accompanying mechanised units during a landing operation, although the impact of the new equipment on its weight, power requirements and ability to operate in water remains unclear.Laser added to an amphibious combat vehicleThe Type 19 family is associated with China’s amphibious forces, and vehicles from the family were reported to have entered service with the 73rd Group Army under the PLA’s Eastern Theatre Command. That command would have a central role in any potential military operation against Taiwan, the South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported.The new variant appears to combine the vehicle’s existing weaponry with a directed-energy system and additional sensors. The arrangement suggests the laser is intended primarily for counter-drone missions, potentially allowing individual armoured vehicles to detect and engage small uncrewed aircraft without relying exclusively on larger air-defense systems.Timothy Heath, founder of defense consultancy Perceptum and a former senior China analyst at RAND and the US military, told SCMP it is difficult to determine from available imagery whether the modifications have affected the vehicle’s amphibious performance. Operating the laser while the vehicle is afloat “should be possible,” although the additional weight and the need to protect the equipment from salt water would have to be addressed, he added.One possible solution could involve reducing the crew or removing other equipment to compensate for the added weight. If those engineering challenges can be overcome, Heath noted the system could be “very useful in a Taiwan conflict”, particularly if Taiwanese forces use drone swarms against PLA vehicles attempting to establish a beachhead.Taiwan is building a larger drone forceThe potential role of the Type 19 variant comes as Taiwan rapidly expands its own use of uncrewed systems. Taiwan’s cabinet has proposed a $4.6 billion supplementary defense budget that includes more than 600 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones and more than 40,000 coastal attack drones. The proposal still requires legislative approval, while lawmakers have also approved a separate $7.6 billion, six-year framework for domestically produced drones.The island has reorganized parts of its military around drone warfare, including the creation of army drone battalions across three operational combat zones. During the Han Kuang 42 exercise in August, Taiwanese units used drones for battlefield surveillance, reconnaissance, intelligence transmission and attack missions.For a PLA force attempting to establish a foothold, drones could be useful not only for attacking vehicles but also for identifying troop positions and movements and directing artillery, missiles and other weapons toward forces operating in exposed areas.That makes vehicle-level counter-drone systems increasingly attractive. The Russia-Ukraine war has demonstrated how inexpensive drones can threaten tanks, artillery and other frontline systems, while the Armenia-Azerbaijan conflict in 2020 showed how uncrewed aircraft can exploit gaps in conventional air defenses.

title: US Marines secure $7.3 million contract for ground robots
content: American Rheinmetall, the US arm of German defense company Rheinmetall, has secured a $7.28 million contract to supply autonomous ground vehicles to the US Marine Corps.The company will manufacture and deliver 12 Mission Master SP Autonomous Unmanned Ground Vehicles (A-UGVs), five amphibious kits, associated Marine Kits, and other supporting equipment. The vehicles will help the service test autonomous logistics and expeditionary mobility technologies.The Defense Logistics Agency is executing the procurement, with military equipment supplier ADS Inc. serving as the prime contractor. The equipment will support the US Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory’s operational evaluations and capability development efforts.Most advanced Mission Master configurationAccording to Rheinmetall, the vehicles represent the most advanced Mission Master configuration it has developed to date. They incorporate the company’s autonomous driving technology and lessons gathered through more than four years of work with the Marine Corps.“This award represents a significant milestone in our long-standing partnership with the United States Marine Corps,” said Matt Warnick, CEO, American Rheinmetall. “For more than four years, we have worked side-by-side with Marines to mature, refine, and advance autonomous ground capabilities. The Mission Master SP captures the full breadth of those lessons learned and showcases Rheinmetall’s commitment to delivering cutting-edge, reliable, and mission-ready autonomous systems,” he added. Pietro Mazzei, president and CEO of Rheinmetall Canada, added, “This collaboration between Rheinmetall colleagues enables the U.S. Marine Corps to deploy the Mission Master SP in the most advanced configuration to date.”“The addition of an amphibious capability marks a significant milestone in ensuring that our system meets the evolving demands of littoral and expeditionary operations,” he added. Amphibious kits for coastal missionsEach Mission Master SP is built around Rheinmetall’s PATH autonomy system, which allows military vehicles to perform tasks with reduced human involvement. The new configuration also includes enhanced vehicle capabilities and support for integrating different mission payloads.Five amphibious kits will allow the unmanned vehicles to operate in water and across coastal environments. This capability is particularly relevant to the Marine Corps, which must move personnel, equipment, and supplies between ships, beaches, and inland positions during expeditionary missions.The vehicles can support logistics without exposing Marines to every hazardous part of a resupply operation. Rheinmetall said the systems could also improve mobility and extend the operational reach of crewed and uncrewed units.Supporting autonomous logistics developmentThe contract covers more than the delivery of the vehicles and kits. Rheinmetall will also provide supporting equipment, program management, training, capability development, and engineering services.American Rheinmetall will lead the work, while Rheinmetall Canada will support the program as the original equipment manufacturer. The vehicles will undergo further experimentation as the Marine Corps explores how autonomous systems can assist distributed forces.The program could also support Rheinmetall’s longer-term plan to expand autonomous vehicle manufacturing in the United States. The company intends to establish an autonomous systems hub focused on production, integration, and future vehicle development.For the Marine Corps, the Mission Master SP offers a platform for examining how unmanned vehicles can carry supplies, improve expeditionary mobility, and limit troop exposure in dangerous environments. The trials will help shape how the service deploys autonomous ground systems during future coastal and battlefield operations.

title: 15 times faster 3D printing tech to build 10,000 drone bodies a month
content: Impossible Objects, an Illinois-based manufacturing technology company, has secured $40 million to expand a high-speed 3D printing system designed for industrial-scale production.The Series B round, led by Inflection Equity, will help the company increase production of its Composite-Based Additive Manufacturing (CBAM) systems. The funds will also support further deployments across aerospace, defense and advanced manufacturing.At the center of the expansion is the CBAM 25, a carbon-fiber printing system that can produce strong, lightweight components without the expensive tooling required by conventional manufacturing processes.From prototyping to mass productionAlthough 3D printing has been available for decades, its industrial use has often remained limited to prototyping. Slow production speeds, material constraints, and high costs have prevented many additive manufacturing systems from competing with CNC machining and injection molding.Impossible Objects claims its CBAM process addresses these limitations by combining rapid production with advanced composite materials, including carbon fiber.The system can manufacture parts for applications traditionally served by established production techniques while reducing tooling requirements, costs, and lead times.“We’ve created a fundamentally new way to manufacture,” said Robert Swartz, founder and chairman of Impossible Objects. “We live our lives through things, and we have changed how things are made. This is as important as the mill, precision measurement, and interchangeable parts. This funding gives us the resources to bring that vision to more customers and make it real at scale,” he added. Printing stronger parts at higher speedsThe CBAM 25 can print as many as 25 layers per minute, making it 15 times faster than competing production additive technologies, according to the company.Its process can produce composite components with strength reaching 200 MPa, which Impossible Objects says is up to four times greater than parts made through rival additive manufacturing methods. The technology also minimizes shrinkage and warpage, two issues that can affect the dimensional accuracy of printed components.Since the system was introduced in early 2025, Impossible Objects has received five orders and begun placing machines with customers and research organizations. These include the U.S. Air Force, the National Institute for Aviation Research, the Oregon Manufacturing Innovation Center, and the Rochester Institute of Technology.“Our CBAM 25 system is designed from the ground up to meet the high productivity and high reliability needs of advanced manufacturing combined with the flexibility and tool-less manufacturing that modern flexible supply chains require,” said Steve Hoover, CEO of Impossible Objects.Supporting drone and aircraft manufacturingThe technology could play a particularly important role in distributed defense production. At the U.S. Army’s Rock Island Arsenal, CBAM can support manufacturing of up to 10,000 drone bodies every month.Impossible Objects has also secured $20 million through U.S. government contracts and awards. Its work covers high-strength long-range drones, lightweight wing and fuselage structures, embedded wiring and additively manufactured components approaching the strength of traditionally produced composites.The latest funding will allow the company to manufacture more CBAM systems, deploy them at additional customer sites, and expand the service and commercial teams supporting its growing installed base.

title: Radia’s WindRunner targets next challenge in space logistics
content:
Designed to move the largest things in the world
“The rockets, boosters, and spacecraft that define the space enterprise’s ambitions keep getting larger, more capable, and more valuable. Yet we’re still relying on transportation
designed decades ago,”
Mark Lundstrom, founder and CEO of Radia.
“WindRunner was designed to move the largest things in the world to the hardest places to reach, and that is exactly what the space community needs. Whether it’s a fully assembled booster, a recovered launch vehicle, or a next generation satellite, we can move it intact, in hours instead of days, without disassembly. With a low cargo deck height, nose door, and an innovative cargo loading system, the WindRunner will enable easier loading of outsized space related cargo. That gives the space enterprise an entirely new logistics capability.”
WindRunner enables a more responsive, resilient, and flexible space mobility
Rather than replacing today’s launch infrastructure or strategic airlift, WindRunner complements and extends both by providing a logistics capability for oversized, volume dominated payloads that no existing aircraft can transport intact. By connecting manufacturing, integration, launch, recovery, and sustainment operations, WindRunner enables a more responsive, resilient, and flexible space mobility architecture for government, allied, and commercial operators.
It’s also revealed that modern space programs increasingly run out of transport options before they run out of ambition.
Rocket stages, boosters, satellites, and other mission critical systems continue to grow in size, while the roads, ports, and aircraft available to move them have remained largely unchanged. As a result, valuable hardware is often disassembled, constrained by existing transportation limits, or routed by sea and road over several days or even weeks, adding cost, schedule risk, and unnecessary handling to some of the world’s most sensitive aerospace systems.
WindRunner can support responsive space operations and enable movement of large launch systems in hours instead of days while supporting the recovery and repositioning of reusable launch vehicles for faster turnaround.
WindRunner offers short takeoff and landing capability from approximately 1,800-meter unpaved runways enables access to emerging spaceports, distributed launch locations, and austere operating sites beyond the reach of conventional cargo aircraft.
WindRunner is designed to operate using standard cargo handling equipment and conventional airfield infrastructure, eliminating the need for specialized loading systems or bespoke facilities.
For military and commercial space operations, this could support a more distributed logistics architecture. Instead of relying exclusively on a small number of major transportation centres, oversized space hardware could potentially be moved closer to emerging spaceports, test facilities or austere operating locations.
Radia says WindRunner could accommodate satellites with roughly twice the dimensional envelope of systems that can currently be transported fully assembled. If that capability becomes practical, spacecraft designers could gain greater freedom to build larger systems without being constrained as heavily by transportation requirements.
That could have applications across communications, Earth observation, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, as well as national-security space missions. In other words, an aircraft designed to solve a logistics problem could potentially influence how future spacecraft themselves are designed.

title: Litavis: World's first spad sensor with on-chip processing
content: Edinburgh-based semiconductor company Singular Photonics has launched Litavis, a new image sensor designed to combine photon counting, timing and statistical analysis directly on a single chip.The company describes Litavis as the world’s first single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) sensor with in-pixel processing capable of combining imaging, timing, histogramming and photon statistics on the same device.Rather than sending large quantities of raw photon data to an external processor, Litavis performs part of the analysis inside the sensor itself. Singular Photonics says this can reduce data transfer requirements and enable lower-latency, more power-efficient imaging systems.A camera that can do more than measure lightSPADs are designed to detect individual photons, making them particularly useful when extremely low light levels or precise measurements of photon arrival times matter.Litavis builds on that sensitivity by making the sensor software-configurable. The same hardware can be reconfigured for different imaging tasks without requiring a new sensor design.Its operating modes include photon-counting imaging, programmable time gating, multiple time-to-digital converter (TDC) configurations, time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC), coincidence detection, and combined timestamping and imaging.This allows the sensor to capture not only how much light reaches each pixel, but also information about when photons arrive and how those events are distributed over time. That additional information can help be applications where conventional intensity-based imaging is not enough.Processing photon events on the chipLitavis uses a CMOS SPAD architecture with digital photon processing integrated directly within the pixel array. The sensor provides continuous 256 × 256-pixel photon-counting imaging under low-light conditions. At the same time, it can generate timestamped photon events on a 64 × 64 macropixel grid, providing picosecond-resolution timing alongside the full-resolution photon-counting image. The device also supports multi-event timing, allowing multiple photons detected during an excitation cycle to be individually assigned to time bins. Its in-pixel histogramming capabilities can then be used to analyze the statistical distribution of those photon events. This opens possibilities beyond conventional camera images, including measurements used in fluorescence lifetime imaging, dynamic light scattering, and quantum sensing, according to Singular Photonics.The approach also addresses a practical problem that can become significant as imaging systems collect more data. Instead of transferring every detected photon event to another processor for analysis, some processing happens within the sensor itself.Singular Photonics says this can reduce the amount of raw data that needs to move through the system, potentially improving latency and power efficiency while allowing real-time processing to scale more effectively.One sensor, multiple applicationsThe company is positioning Litavis as a flexible platform rather than a sensor designed around one particular application. Potential uses include machine vision, robotics, physical AI, depth sensing, spectroscopy, scientific and medical imaging, quantum technologies and industrial automation.The software-configurable architecture is intended to let developers and system integrators experiment with different acquisition and timing modes using the same hardware. That could reduce the need to develop separate sensor architectures for different applications and shorten development cycles.“Litavis combines the sensitivity advantages of SPAD technology with the adaptability and scalability increasingly required by modern multimodal imaging,” said Shahida Imani, CEO of Singular Photonics.Singular Photonics says it has already received significant pre-orders from companies and institutions internationally. The company plans to demonstrate Litavis at SPIE Sensors + Imaging in Edinburgh and later at VISION in Stuttgart, giving developers an opportunity to see the sensor’s multimodal capabilities in operation.Instead of treating the image sensor as a device that simply captures photons and leaves all interpretation to a computer, Litavis attempts to move some of that intelligence into the sensor itself.

title: Iran-linked actor used Claude AI to track US Navy ships
content: An Iran-linked actor used Anthropic’s Claude AI to collect publicly available information on U.S. Navy forces and develop targeting recommendations, according to a new report from the AI company. Anthropic says it detected and disrupted the operation before banning the account and sharing information with government authorities.The disclosure highlights a growing problem for military planners: the same AI systems being developed to process enormous amounts of information for legitimate uses can also help adversaries turn scattered public data into actionable intelligence.According to Anthropic, the Iranian-linked actor used Claude to build an automated pipeline that assembled targeting handbooks from ship and aircraft transponder identifiers, commercial satellite imagery and photographs of U.S. military personnel. The actor also used the model to research vulnerabilities in shipboard systems, including maritime satellite terminals, Cisco communications equipment and industrial-control products.AI is becoming part of the targeting processAnthropic’s report is significant not because Iran has suddenly discovered AI, but because it shows how a commercially available generative AI system can compress parts of an intelligence workflow that previously required considerable specialist effort.Claude apparently wasn’t used to launch an attack autonomously. Instead, Anthropic says it used it to collect, organize, and analyze information, automate open-source intelligence work, and produce material that could support military planning. The Wall Street Journal first reported the findings, which Anthropic detailed in its latest report on the misuse of its AI models.Modern targeting is increasingly a data-processing problem, with forces having to sift through satellite imagery, drone video, electronic signals, communications and other sources faster than human analysts can manage alone.The United States has been pursuing this approach for years. The Pentagon’s Project Maven, for example, was created to use machine learning and computer vision to process imagery and identify objects of military interest. U.S. Army publications say newer Maven systems can scan large quantities of imagery, flag potential targets, and feed information into existing targeting workflows, with human analysts responsible for validation.The Army has continued to expand these capabilities. In a 2026 exercise, the service described Maven Smart System as an AI-enabled tool that can process thousands of hours of surveillance video and automatically identify and flag objects of interest.In other words, AI-assisted targeting is not uniquely Iranian, Chinese, or Russian. It is becoming part of military modernization across major powers.Epic Fury shows why human oversight mattersThe issue has become particularly sensitive following the February 28 U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. A U.S. strike hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, killing at least 168 people, according to reporting by The Associated Press, most of them children. The Washington Post subsequently reported that the school had appeared on a U.S. target list and may have been mistakenly identified as a military site. The Post also reported that questions had been raised about whether AI-assisted target identification played a role, but that does not establish that AI caused the strike or that an AI system selected the school as a target.Israel has also incorporated AI-assisted systems into its military operations. Since the military campaign in Gaza began, reporting has examined systems such as Lavender, which Israeli officials have described as an analytical aid rather than an autonomous target-selection system.Reuters reported in 2024 that the United States was examining allegations that Israel had used AI to identify bombing targets, while the Israeli military said human analysts remained responsible for target identification and decisions. These examples do not make Iran’s reported use of Claude less concerning. They illustrate why the issue extends beyond any single country.Claude was also used for weapons and surveillance effortsThe Iranian naval operation was one of several cases described in Anthropic’s 154-page report covering activity between December 2025 and August 2026. The company says users in northern Yemen attempted to use Claude to develop software for advanced missile systems. Anthropic says it blocked some requests, but others passed its safeguards before it banned the accounts.The report also describes Chinese government-aligned operations that allegedly used Claude for surveillance and profiling, including efforts targeting Uyghurs and religious figures. Russian-linked actors, meanwhile, reportedly attempted to use Claude to develop autonomous drone swarms using data from the war in Ukraine.Anthropic says it disrupted all of the operations described in the report and has since strengthened its detection systems. The cases demonstrate an uncomfortable reality for the AI industry: preventing dangerous use is not simply a matter of refusing an obviously malicious question. Anthropic says some actors deliberately fragmented their requests into individually benign tasks, allowing them to assemble more dangerous capabilities over multiple interactions.As AI systems become better at coding, research, image analysis and handling large datasets, the military significance of those general-purpose capabilities will continue to grow. The central question, therefore, is no longer whether AI will be used in warfare. It already is. The more consequential question is how much authority humans will retain over the systems helping them find, prioritize, and ultimately engage targets, and whether those safeguards will be strong enough when the data feeding the machines is incomplete, misleading, or simply wrong.

title: Scientists Turn Common Plastic Waste Into Fuel Using Heated Salts
content:
Chemistry
A molten-salt process could turn common polyethylene waste into fuel at unusually low temperatures. Credit: Stock
Common plastic waste could become fuel using heated salts instead of extreme temperatures.
Plastic bags, cutting boards, and many other everyday products are made from a plastic that is notoriously difficult to reuse once it becomes waste. Researchers at
Oak Ridge National Laboratory
have now found a way to break down this plastic and turn it into gasoline-like and diesel-like fuels using a relatively simple mixture of heated salts.
The plastic is polyethylene, one of the most widely used plastics in the world. In laboratory experiments, the new process converted it at temperatures below 200 degrees Celsius (392 degrees Fahrenheit), far cooler than many conventional methods, and produced a gasoline yield of about 60%.
The method also avoided several ingredients commonly needed to turn plastic into fuel. It did not require expensive precious metal catalysts, organic solvents, or an outside supply of hydrogen.
Molten salts replace harsher chemistry
At the heart of the process are molten salts containing aluminum chloride. Molten salts are simply salts heated until they form a liquid. In this case, the liquid salt mixture served both as the environment where the reaction took place and as the catalyst that helped drive it.
“We converted polymer waste to value-added fuels by using commercially available inorganic salts as the reaction media to provide the catalytic sites,” said Zhenzhen Yang, an ORNL staff scientist who was also a co-corresponding author of the paper. “Unlike traditional techniques for converting polymer to fuel, the new process did not require noble-metal catalysts, organic solvents or external hydrogen. This is the first time molten salts were used as media to produce high-value-added chemicals from waste without any catalytic initiator or solvent and at temperature below 200 degrees Celsius.”
A novel molten salt-based system converts polyethylene waste into gasoline- and diesel-like fuels for transportation and manufacturing. Credit: Jacquelyn DeMink/ORNL, U.S. Dept. of Energy
The relatively low temperature is an important part of the approach. A common method called pyrolysis breaks plastics apart with intense heat, typically at about 450 to 500 degrees Celsius (842 to 932 degrees Fahrenheit).
“We developed an efficient and selective polyethylene-to-gasoline conversion,” said Liqi Qiu, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who performed most of the study’s experiments in the ORNL laboratory of Sheng Dai, of ORNL and UTK. Dai, an ORNL Corporate Fellow and section head for separations and polymer chemistry, is a co-corresponding author of the paper.
Aluminum sites break plastic chains apart
The researchers also wanted to understand why the molten salts worked.
Polyethylene is made from long chains of carbon and hydrogen atoms. The team found that aluminum sites in the molten salt become strongly acidic and can trigger reactions that break those long chains into smaller hydrocarbon molecules, the kinds of compounds found in fuels.
One key step involves the formation of a positively charged carbon atom. To follow what happened during that reaction, the researchers used deuterium, a heavier form of hydrogen, as a chemical marker.
They then turned to neutron scattering at ORNL’s Spallation Neutron Source, which is especially useful for tracking hydrogen and its isotopes.
“The polymer contains a lot of hydrogen,” Dai said. “Neutrons are ideal at discerning light elements including hydrogen and its isotopes, such as deuterium.”
Those measurements helped explain why different forms of polyethylene produced different kinds of fuel. Simpler polymer chains tended to produce gasoline-like compounds, while more complex chains generated diesel-like products.
The researchers also examined what happened to the aluminum catalyst itself during the reaction. At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s Advanced Light Source, Yang worked with Min-Jae Kim and Jinhua Guo to use soft X-rays to study changes in the aluminum sites as they interacted with polyethylene.
“The aluminum edge shifted to the low-electron-density edge, which means some electron-rich intermediates formed,” Yang said. “We compared the findings with other techniques and confirmed an aromatic ring intermediate can coordinate with aluminum and cause a binding-energy change.”
The measurements provided evidence that the aluminum sites were actively driving the reaction. The team supported those findings with several additional techniques, including nuclear magnetic resonance, X-ray diffraction, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and computer simulations.
Decades of molten salt research find a new use
The work draws on decades of molten salt research at Oak Ridge. ORNL has studied these materials since at least the 1960s, when its Molten Salt Reactor Experiment demonstrated their potential for use in nuclear reactors. Dai later proposed applying molten salt chemistry to a very different challenge: converting discarded polymers into useful products.
Molten salts can remain stable under demanding chemical conditions, which could make them attractive for industrial processing if the new method can eventually be scaled up.
“The ORNL system solves two fundamental issues,” Dai said. “One, for a stable system, the process can be radically easier to scale up. Two, the previous system needed an initiator to kick off catalytic reactions. However, the ORNL system does not need one.”
Understanding the underlying chemistry could also help researchers apply the approach to other plastics or chemical processes.
“In this case we tackled polyethylene, a widely available commodity polymer, using molten salt,” said ORNL’s Tomonori Saito, who managed the project and contributed expertise in polymers. “We’re trying to understand fundamental science that will lead to discoveries and new economic opportunities.”
Water remains a barrier to scale-up
The method still has an important drawback. The aluminum-based molten salt readily absorbs water, which makes the system less stable. The researchers now hope to develop ways to better contain and protect the molten salts, potentially using halogens or carbon-based materials to improve separation and processing.
If those challenges can be overcome and the process can be scaled beyond the laboratory, discarded polyethylene could become a source of useful fuel-like chemicals rather than remaining difficult plastic waste. The team has
applied for a patent
on the method.
“Polymer source material is abundantly available from consumer waste, and our catalyst system, aluminum molten salts, is very cheap,” Qiu said. “This advance may be promising for industry.”
Reference: “Polyethylene Upcycling to Liquid Alkanes in Molten Salts under Neat and External Hydrogen Source-Free Conditions” by Liqi Qiu, Felipe Polo-Garzon, Luke L. Daemen, Min-Jae Kim, Jinghua Guo, Bobby G. Sumpter, Michael R. Koehler, Carlos Alberto Steren, Tao Wang, Logan T Kearney, Tomonori Saito, Zhenzhen Yang and Sheng Dai, 7 April 2025, Journal of the American Chemical Society.
DOI: 10.1021/jacs.5c01107
The DOE Office of Science (Materials Sciences and Engineering Division) primarily supported the research as well as the gas chromatography-mass spectrometry work (Chemical Sciences, Geosciences and Biosciences Division, Catalysis Science program).
